S7 PvP Teams Counters Maps Heroes Caveats

AFK Journey Season 7 PvP report

Team groups, counters and map records from Supreme League and Guild Duel matches.

Everything here, including the written insights, was produced by an automated analysis of saved tournament results and hero skill descriptions. No replays were reviewed, so explanations of wins and losses have not been checked against what happened during a battle, such as targeting or ability timing. Most records come from top-spending players at the top end of the meta, with heavily upgraded rosters. The interpretations can be wrong, and results may differ with fewer upgrades. More about the data's limits.

Last updated 2026-09-22 · Season 7 records

1 · Team groups #

A team group contains related five-hero lineups that share heroes. Its name lists the heroes those lineups share. heroes appear most often; heroes vary between lineups. Icon percentages show how often each hero appears. Every hero that appears often enough to count as core or flex is shown. Groups are sorted by strength tier, then by appearances. Strength estimates how often the team would beat an average team when both sides have equal upgrades, allowing for the opponents it actually faced and the upgrade gaps recorded. The full ratings include the unadjusted rating and the figures each tier is based on, and explains the cutoffs.

excludes ties. The bar below it shows the 95% interval, the range the true win rate most likely falls in, with a dot for the win rate and a tick at 50%. A wider segment means less certainty; it does not account for differences in players, upgrades or repeated teams. shows how often the most popular artifact is equipped.

Insights

Place Gwyneth behind Gunnar and include Dunlingr high confidence

Gwyneth stands directly behind Gunnar on 494 of 500 boards fielding both. Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is 243–115 with Dunlingr and 63–57 without him.

What to do Keep Gwyneth behind Gunnar and prioritize Dunlingr when the opponent may use Saida/Contess/Twins or Thador/Solise.

Gunnar gives the ally directly behind him extra range, attack and steadfast. That placement is part of the skill, so keep her behind him when changing the formation. Dunlingr blocks enemy ultimates at battle start. His Bell has one mode, chosen before battle, and players usually pick Spellbind. Gwyneth relies on normal attacks while many opposing teams need their first ultimates.

With Dunlingr, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is 42–6 against Saida/Contess/Twins and 24–0 against Thador/Solise. Different players and opponents can affect those records, but his ultimate block gives a reason to favor this version against teams that need early casts.

Alna/Syph/Mehira needs the Winter Warrior buff on Sylphira and a path to the enemy medium confidence

Alna/Syph/Mehira is 62–37 with Zandrok in Supreme League and 71–57 without him; the Guild Duel records are 32–22 and 18–16–1t.

What to do Place Sylphira so she receives Winter Warrior. Favor Zandrok where his Haste buff and wall destruction help the team reach the enemy.

Alna slows her own allies as well as the enemy. Her Winter Warrior is the closest ally in her diagonal row (the frontmost one if two are equally close). That ally escapes the Haste reduction and gains max HP. Across 521 Alna boards, Sylphira receives it 324 times, going 192–131 with a tie. The thirteen boards with nobody in the row went 3–10.

Zandrok helps the rest of the melee team with opening Haste and max HP, and his charge destroys breakable walls. That clears a route to the enemy and can remove a wall placed by Kulu. Obstacles that cannot be broken stay in place. A battle-start charm from Mehira can interrupt his roar, so when both teams use Alna, check whether Mehira can interrupt Zandrok at battle start.

Evie/Orion benefits from Rolan but struggles when enemies stop its ultimates medium confidence

Evie/Orion is 122–71–1t with Rolan and 57–81–1t without him.

What to do Use allies that cast ultimates frequently and keep Orion and Perseus safe so they can deal damage. Adding Rolan does not make the team reliable against Contess or Dunlingr.

Rolan supplies temporary buffs for Orion and benefits from frequent allied ultimates. Those casts also protect Evie: each ally ultimate lowers her Detection meter, keeping her concealed longer. Contess and Saida interfere with the casting that makes this work, while Dunlingr can prevent the opening ultimates. Orion is 22–56 with two ties against boards containing Contess, and 19–45 against boards containing Dunlingr. The better record with Rolan is a reason to include him, but he does not fix the team’s bad matchups.

Check the format before adding Rolan to Saida/Contess/Twins medium confidence

The Rolan version is 28–7–1t in Supreme League but 9–7 in Guild Duel.

What to do Practice the Rolan version, but place it where it is less likely to face Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu and check its Guild Duel record separately.

Saida/Contess/Twins punishes enemy ultimate casts while supplying its own healing and Energy. Rolan can help that team, but its strong Supreme League record does not show that it does as well in Guild Duel. Check which opposing teams it would face and whether another team in your set needs Rolan more.

Check Gerda’s partner in Saida/Contess/Twins medium confidence

With Gerda and Solise, the exact team is 9–21–2t across 20 players. Its frequent use is not a reason to copy it.

What to do If Gerda is part of this team, test Aliceth as her partner before copying the common Solise version.

Keeping Gerda and using Aliceth instead, the team is 24–17–1t across 11 players. With similar upgrades, the Solise version is 3–8 and the Aliceth version is 10–6.

These results compare different players, opponents and formations, so they do not prove Aliceth causes the improvement. They do make the Aliceth version a more promising starting point to test. Check whether Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu already needs her before assigning the full set.

Rolan and the twins: choose supporting heroes your other teams can spare medium confidence

Rolan/Twins boards vary their supporting heroes, and the usual ones are also needed by other main teams.

What to do Check all five heroes on a board before using its record, and decide which team gets Sylphira, Contess or Mehira before choosing the other teams.

Sylphira is on 52% of its boards, Contess on 47%, Mehira on 38%, Taichi & Agumon on 37% and Athalia on 32%. A Sylphira version takes Sylphira away from Alna/Syph/Mehira; a Contess version takes Contess away from Saida/Contess/Twins. Choose the version as part of your full set.

In Supreme League the boards with Contess are 28–5–2t and the boards without her 28–18; the boards with Sylphira are 30–15 and the boards without her 26–8–2t. Those with-and-without records come from different players and opponents, and the counter records add every version together, so check which supporting heroes the recorded wins used before copying one.

Avoid sending Rolan/Twins into an expected Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu on SL map 5 medium confidence

Rolan/Twins is 12–12 on SL map 5: 0–6 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, but 12–6 against other teams.

What to do Check the opposing team before assigning Rolan/Twins to map 5. If Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is likely there, try another matchup and recheck the rest of your set.

Its map 5 record is level only because of that one matchup. It does not show that the arena itself is bad for Rolan. These are small samples with different players, upgrades and supporting heroes; moving the same lineup elsewhere does not guarantee a win.

Thador/Solise struggles against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu even with the usual formation medium confidence

Keep Frieren, Thador and Solise each within one tile of Himmel to form his party. That formation still needs a favorable opponent.

What to do Keep Frieren, Thador and Solise each within one tile of Himmel. Avoid placing Thador/Solise where it may face Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, even if your heroes have more upgrades.

Across boards fielding all four, the party is formed on 116 boards at 55–61; the five boards that break it are 0–5. The skill requires that placement; the five losses alone cannot show how much it improves results. Lily May can interrupt an early opposing ultimate, but cannot stop Gwyneth’s normal attacks. See the counter results before assigning this team to an opponent.

Try Frieren with Alna, Sylphira, Mehira and Zandrok if she is available low confidence

This exact lineup is 15–1, including 9–1 with similar upgrades, but only 3 players used it.

What to do Test the Frieren version against your expected opponent if your other teams can spare her. Keep Sylphira receiving Alna’s Winter Warrior buff.

One player accounts for 11 of its 16 appearances; the other two went 4–1. The result is worth testing, but opponents, placement and player differences could explain part of it.

With Hepler in Frieren’s place, the same four heroes are 15–17 across 15 players, and 9–9 with similar upgrades. More players used the Hepler version, but the two records come from different players and opponents, so they do not show what swapping the one hero does. Frieren may also be needed alongside Himmel and Thador/Solise in your set.

Counters with statistical support #

A losing record alone does not establish a counter. The team may struggle against many opponents or on that particular map. The test compares its record against this opponent with its record against everyone else on the same maps, then combines those comparisons. Each game's upgrade gap also counts. Losing while far behind on paragon and refinement is weaker evidence of a counter, and winning from behind is stronger evidence. Games with teams from the same group on both sides are excluded. A map where the team faced only one opponent is left out, because there is no other record there to compare against.

Near level keeps only games with an upgrade gap below 4.5 points, combining paragon and refinement. It helps show whether the losing record also appears when upgrades are similar. Player skill and team differences can still affect it. Win-rate gap is the difference between the two win rates, in percentage points.

The p-value is how often a gap this large would appear by chance if there were no special matchup effect, after allowing for maps and upgrade gaps. The smaller it is, the less likely the gap is chance alone, as long as the test's assumptions hold. It is not the probability that a counter is false.

12 matchups have statistical support; 7 more are possible but unconfirmed.

Counter results by map, format, player and team version

Alna/Syph/Mehira beats Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu

On the maps where they met, Gunnar / Gwyneth / Kulu wins 75% of its games against everyone else but 35% against Alna/Syph/Mehira. That is 25 wins; going by the maps and upgrade gaps alone, about 42 would be expected if there were no special matchup effect. The test accounting for maps and upgrade gaps gives a p-value of under 1 in 1,000. Counted by whole matches instead of games it is 42–21 with 3 split to Alna/Syph/Mehira, from 66 separate matches between 55 pairs of players.

Insights

Six counters have stronger statistical evidence high confidence

Alna/Syph/Mehira over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Saida/Contess/Twins, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Evie/Orion, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Thador/Solise, Evie/Orion over Zorya/Athalia/Pandora and Zorya/Athalia/Pandora over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu pass the stricter test, the one the report uses because it compares 76 pairings at once and some of them would look one-sided by chance alone. Evie/Orion over Alna/Syph/Mehira, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Rolan/Twins, Rolan/Twins over Evie/Orion and Saida/Contess/Twins over Evie/Orion pass only the usual test, where a record this one-sided would come up by chance less than one time in twenty (0.05). Alna/Athalia/Eryndor over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu and Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Evie/Orion/Hepler pass that usual test too, each from fewer than eight games. The test weighs each game by its upgrade gap, so a win taken while behind on upgrades counts for more than one taken while ahead.

What to do Use these counters when choosing teams for a likely matchup. Rolan/Twins still needs more games against Evie/Orion with similar upgrades.

The counter table gives the records and near-level comparisons. The six stronger results hold whatever value in its likely range is used for how much an upgrade gap matters. Evie/Orion over Alna/Syph/Mehira passes the usual test across that range but not the stricter one: a record this one-sided would come up by chance about 15 times in 10,000 (0.0015), and the stricter test allows fewer than 7 in 10,000 (0.00066). Evie/Orion against Zorya/Athalia/Pandora is 26–0, with 8–0 of those games near level. Rolan/Twins against Evie/Orion is 15–4 but only 3–1 with similar upgrades, so do not count on the overall record until more games with similar upgrades are recorded.

The heroes’ skills explain why each of these counters works. Alna slows the Gunnar pair while Sylphira attacks its clustered backline; Zandrok helps the melee team reach it. Dunlingr stops the opening ultimates Saida/Contess/Twins and Thador/Solise need. His block also stops the ally ultimates that keep Evie hidden, while Gwyneth’s normal attacks are unaffected. Orion is 19–45 against boards with Dunlingr and 23–45 against boards with Gwyneth. Contess punishes casts and Saida drains Energy, undermining the allied ultimates that keep Evie concealed. Zorya does nothing until her Energy is full, so a team that attacks early can kill her supporting heroes before her ultimate is ready. A statistical label only describes the games already recorded; it does not guarantee the next one.

Evidence Stricter cut-off used because 76 pairings were compared at once: 0.05 / 76 = 0.00066

In Ro4 and Finals, move Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu if the opponent can field Zorya/Athalia/Pandora medium confidence

In SL5’s Ro4 and Finals, where each match is drafted separately, Zorya/Athalia/Pandora met Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu in 11 games and went 9–2, including 8–1 while behind on upgrades. Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu was 29–26 in those rounds, compared with 108–57 from Group to Ro16.

What to do Before Ro4 and Finals, check whether the opponent has used Zorya/Athalia/Pandora. If so, do not leave Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu on its usual map: put Evie/Orion or Saida/Contess/Twins there and recheck the other four maps.

From Group to Ro16 a player keeps one set for the whole stage, so nobody can choose a team for one opponent. In Ro4 and Finals the opponent drafts against you and can see where you placed Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu all season. Zorya/Athalia/Pandora was used against it by 8 players in those rounds, and was in 30 of 62 of the sets drafted for them. Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu was on map 5 in 19 of its 55 appearances there and on map 4 in 12.

Zorya/Athalia/Pandora loses to Evie/Orion and Saida/Contess/Twins, as the Zorya/Athalia/Pandora note in this box shows. If the opponent has used Zorya/Athalia/Pandora, put one of those two teams on the map where you usually place Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu and move Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu to another map. Its record against Evie/Orion also fell to 5–8 in those rounds, from 18–5 earlier in SL5; thirteen games are too few to say that counter stops working.

Evidence Limits: Eleven games from several leagues of one league season. SL4’s Ro4 and Finals had Zorya/Athalia/Pandora in 7 of 28 sets and it never met Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, so the pattern has been seen once.

Evie/Orion has a winning record against Alna/Syph/Mehira, but check the formation medium confidence

Evie/Orion is 28–17 against Alna/Syph/Mehira and 12–6 with similar upgrades. After allowing for map and upgrade differences, the result passes the usual test for chance but just misses the stricter one used because many pairings were compared at once.

What to do Use Evie against an expected Alna, and compare the exact formation with a practiced mirror before committing the set.

Evie can begin inside the enemy half while invincible, which gives a reason for the pairing. The near-level games are far fewer than the overall record, so compare this formation with using Alna/Syph/Mehira yourself, if you have practiced it (see the mirror insight), and check the map and upgrade differences before relying on it.

Zorya/Athalia/Pandora beats Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu while behind on upgrades, but struggles badly against other teams low confidence

Zorya/Athalia/Pandora is 22–18 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, and 17–9 in the games where it was behind on upgrades, so the test that counts each game by its upgrade gap strongly supports the counter. With similar upgrades it is only 3–6, so the wins that make it a counter came in games where the Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu side had more upgrades.

What to do Use Zorya only for a specific expected matchup with a team you have practiced. Check whether the opponent can respond with Evie/Orion or Saida/Contess/Twins.

Its Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu results also differ by map: 6–3 on SL map 1, 7–4 on SL map 2 and 6–3 across the current SL maps 3 and 4, but 2–6 on SL map 5. Practice the intended formation and arena before using it as an alternative to Alna/Syph/Mehira.

It is 0–26 against Evie/Orion and 0–15 against Saida/Contess/Twins. Before choosing Zorya against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, check whether the set can still win if the opponent changes the order and Zorya faces one of those teams.

Insights

Choose your SL map 5 team expecting Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu opposite it medium confidence

Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is on 127 of 402 recorded SL map 5 boards, more than it has on any other map, and is 91–36 there.

What to do If you do not know where the opponent places Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, assume map 5. Put Alna/Syph/Mehira or your own Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu there, and place Saida/Contess/Twins, Thador/Solise and Rolan/Twins on other maps.

Saida/Contess/Twins and Rolan/Twins win only about half their map 5 games because they meet Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu there: each has a clear winning record against every other team on map 5. See the Saida/Contess/Twins note in this box and the Rolan/Twins note in the team group insights. Those records do not show that the arena itself is bad for them. Thador/Solise is 0–6 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu on map 5.

Alna/Syph/Mehira, a supported counter to Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, is 18–10 on map 5 and 5–5 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu there, which is a small sample. Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu also appears on every other map, so map 5 is only the most likely place to meet it.

Place Saida/Contess/Twins on SL map 1, 2 or 4 medium confidence

Saida/Contess/Twins is 24–19 on map 1, 24–13–2t on map 2 and 29–17–8t on the current map 4, but 21–24–4t on the current map 3 and only 28–29–2t on map 5.

What to do Start Saida/Contess/Twins on map 1, 2 or 4. Move it to map 3 or map 5 only when you expect the opponent’s Alna/Syph/Mehira and Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu on other maps.

Each of the two weaker records comes mostly from one opposing team. On map 5 Saida/Contess/Twins is 4–15 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu and 24–14–2t against every other team. On the current map 3 it is 1–6 against Alna/Syph/Mehira and 20–18–4t against every other team.

Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Saida/Contess/Twins is a supported counter in the counter table. Alna/Syph/Mehira over Saida/Contess/Twins is not a supported counter. Across all maps Alna/Syph/Mehira is 24–22–1t against it, so the map 3 result is seven games that could easily go the other way. Saida/Contess/Twins is the most-used team on the current map 3, with 49 of 346 boards, and Alna/Syph/Mehira has 38 of 346.

Thador/Solise has a losing record on every current SL map medium confidence

Thador/Solise is the most-used team on the current map 4, with 78 of 346 boards, and is 31–44–3t there.

What to do Do not choose map 4 for Thador/Solise because other players put it there. If it is your fifth team, assign your four stronger teams to their maps first, give it the map that is left, and treat it as the first team to replace.

It is also 9–15 on map 1, 13–16 on map 2, 18–29 on the current map 3 and 6–17 on map 5. Its winning records, 11–4 and 10–9, are on the map 3 and map 4 arenas used from SL1 to SL3. Moving it to another map has not fixed its results; the opposing team matters more, as the Thador/Solise note in the team group insights explains.

An opponent’s Thador/Solise is most likely on map 4. On that arena Alna/Syph/Mehira is 7–2 against it, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu 6–0 and Evie/Orion 4–2. These are small samples from different players and upgrades.

Heroes that only one team can use

Rolan and Rowan support Evie/Orion here, Zandrok stays with Alna/Syph/Mehira, and Dunlingr stays with Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu. Aliceth goes to Saida/Contess/Twins, so Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu takes Cyran as its fifth hero. Replacing one team can force a change in another: a Rolan/Twins team would take Rolan from Evie/Orion, and its usual versions also take Sylphira or Mehira from Alna/Syph/Mehira.

How an opponent who knows this set could beat it

Rearranging the five teams of one recorded SL set puts a supported counter against four of these teams: Rolan/Twins on map 1, Evie/Orion on map 3, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu on map 4, Alna/Athalia/Eryndor on map 5. Those opposing teams would still need testing on their new maps. Any set can be countered this way once the opponent knows it. Before submitting your teams, test them against the opponent’s teams in a changed order and against teams chosen to beat yours. If two maps look likely to lose, the other three must all win.

4 · Heroes #

Rolan: skills and placement #

The three most-used tiles on each current SL map, as a share of Rolan's appearances there. Where the hero stood on the enemy side of the map, its tile is flipped to the matching tile on the ally side, so both sides count together.

How his skills work
A Celestial support whose skills all work off a team Morale meter. Battle starts at 20% Morale, or more when the team uses heroes from one faction, most of all Lightbearers or Celestials, who also take 50% less damage for 8s. Every 20% Morale gives every ally ATK worth 10% of Rolan's. Every ally ultimate adds 10% (Elijah & Lailah's ultimate counts twice), each kill adds 10% and each death takes 10% off. If Rolan dies the meter is wiped.
At 60% Morale
His blessing on the two highest-damage allies (control-immune for 10s, +ATK) adds 50 Haste, and his heal also stuns the enemies in the spot where most of them stand together, for 3s.
At 100% Morale
A radiant ward: each ally ultimate spawns a clone that casts it again, Morale can no longer drop while he lives, and allies inside are immune to stat reductions.
Ultimate
Cleanses allies, equalizes their HP percentages, grants +150% max HP decaying over 12s and a large heal, plus 15% Morale.

Skills from the app's text for Rolan; numbers rounded. The insights below explain how these skills affect team choices.

Placement advice

Placing Rolan farther back may help, but does not guarantee a win medium confidence

Back-row placements have winning records, but the direct comparison between teams that both used Rolan is too close to establish that farther back is better.

What to do Place Rolan where his allies can protect him from the enemy’s opening attacks. The back corner is not always safest.

His death removes Morale, so protection matters. The two Rolans can also have different teammates. A corner can expose him to enemies that target the rearmost hero; check those skills and his allies’ protection before moving him farther back.

Evidence Rows from center: 4 rows 93–46–2t; 3 rows 113–43–2t; 2 rows 46–31; 1 row 1–2; center row 11–12 · Both teams used Rolan: Rolan farther back won 17 of 28

Using the same team group as the opponent needs practice and an upgrade check medium confidence

The player with the higher overall win rate won 108 of 153 decided mirrors within named team groups. That overall win rate includes these same games. Part of it is the mirror results themselves, so it is only a rough measure of skill. Where a mirror had an upgrade gap of at least one level, the side with more upgrades went 66–16 with three ties.

What to do Practice the full formation and compare both sides’ upgrades before choosing the same team group as the opponent.

Using the same team group as the opponent is an option when no counter is established, but those observations do not make it an automatic win for the stronger player. The two teams can still differ in supporting heroes, placement and what happens at battle start. Private 1v1 tests can help compare one supporting-hero change with everything else kept the same. They do not replace tournament games, and they do not show how badly the set could do against an opponent who has chosen teams to beat it.

Gwyneth: skills and placement #

The three most-used tiles on each current SL map, as a share of Gwyneth's appearances there. Where the hero stood on the enemy side of the map, its tile is flipped to the matching tile on the ally side, so both sides count together.

How her skills work
A Lightbearer marksman whose damage comes from her normal attacks, which run in a cycle of three. The second arrow deals heavy fire damage and burns the target, lowering its Vitality; the third silences the target for 1s and splashes lightning over every enemy within 2 tiles, stunning them briefly. With her Exclusive Equipment the first arrow carries both effects and all her normal attacks deal 20–30% more; at its third level that arrow also strikes for 10% of the target's max HP and ignores most of its physical defense.
Ultimate
Rains arrows over the tile with the most enemies and every tile within 2 of it, immobilizing them for 2s. Her charged normal attack also hits harder the more attack speed and Haste she has.
Distance
Hero Focus gives her attack speed during battle and more of it when no enemy has been within 1 tile of her for 3s; her Enhance Force awakening then shortens the gap between her normal attacks by 40% under the same condition. Everything in her kit rewards standing where enemies cannot reach her quickly, and Gunnar's bonus range to the ally directly behind him lets her hit from there.

Skills from the app's text for Gwyneth; numbers rounded.

Team and placement advice

Gwyneth, Gunnar, Kulu and Dunlingr with Aliceth is the best-supported version high confidence

The Aliceth line-up is 59–18 across 22 players and 29–10 with similar upgrades. The Cyran line-up is 30–15, and 11–2 with similar upgrades.

What to do Start from Gwyneth, Gunnar, Kulu, Dunlingr and Aliceth. Use Cyran as the fifth hero when Aliceth is needed elsewhere, and favor Dunlingr against teams that need early ultimates.

Favor Dunlingr against teams that need opening ultimates: across both formats the team group is 243–115 with him and 63–57 without him. These raw records mix in the effect of upgrades, teammates and opponents, so they do not show how much he adds by himself. Kulu is on most boards and in both leading line-ups, and his wall changes the enemy’s paths, but the team also wins without him: in Supreme League the team group is 196–102 with Kulu and 38–22 without him.

Aliceth has the largest sample and the widest use. Peggy is 17–4, but only three players used her and just 3–1 is near level. That higher raw win rate does not make her the safer choice. Contess (22–6) and Frieren (20–13) were used mostly in Guild Duel; check the flex options under Common variations in the team group’s profile when choosing alternatives.

Evidence Line-ups compared: the 12 most-used exact line-ups, out of 77 recorded

Keep Gwyneth in the back two rows, directly behind Gunnar high confidence

Inside Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu she is 274–137 in the back two rows and 22–31 one row further forward.

What to do Place Gunnar in the third row from the center line or deeper, with Gwyneth directly behind him. Bringing her forward to reach a target loses the attack speed her skills depend on.

Hero Focus always grants attack speed. Its extra bonus and her awakening’s 40% shorter time between attacks require 3 seconds without an enemy within 1 tile. A protected back-row tile helps her keep those bonuses. Gunnar gives the ally directly behind him extra range, attack and steadfast, which is why she stands there on almost every board. When you move the pair, move them together.

Evidence Directly behind Gunnar: 465 of 470 boards inside the team group

Evie: where to start her on each Supreme League map #

How her skills work
When the battle starts, Intel Chase teleports Evie to the tile on the enemy half that mirrors her own and hides her there, invincible. She immediately gathers intel on every enemy hero within 1 tile of where she lands, then on the rest one at a time from nearest to farthest, 4.5s each, gaining 150 Energy per hero. Her Detection meter fills at 120 a second and every ally ultimate takes 500 off it; at 1000 she is revealed where she stands and loses her invincibility. Once every enemy is investigated she teleports back to her own tile.
Why the landing tile matters
Without ally ultimates she has about 8s hidden. Enemies next to her landing tile are investigated together in the first 4.5s; each enemy farther away costs another 4.5s. Every investigated hero loses 20% Magic DEF for the battle. If she investigates all of them while still hidden, every enemy loses another 25% and deals 25–35% less damage through her Exclusive Equipment, and with her awakening she gains a second healing quill. Landing next to the enemy line is how she finishes in time.
Active skills
Her ultimate interrogates the enemy with the most damage dealt, immobilizing it for 6–8s and silencing it if already investigated; Pointed Proof dashes to the nearest enemy for two dagger strikes; Foretold Favor's quill heals and buffs the ally dealing the most damage.

Skills from the app's text for Evie; numbers rounded. The landing tile is the tile on the enemy half that matches hers after the board is turned halfway around, the same rule this report uses to mirror enemy positions.

Amber tiles are her three most-used starts on each map, with her record from each. The blue tile is the start whose landing tile has had the most enemy heroes next to it, averaged over every enemy formation recorded on that map, whatever team Evie's side played. It is drawn as a blue border when it is also one of her starts. The opponent's team changes where enemies stand, so the blue tile only shows where enemies usually are; check the actual formation when you know it.

Placement advice

Start Evie where her landing tile touches the enemy line medium confidence

Averaged over all recorded enemy formations on each SL arena, tile 4’s landing spot has 2.7, 2.9 and 3.1 enemies next to it on maps 1, 2 and 3. These averages include games without Evie. On map 5, tile 3 touches only 1.4 enemies on average.

What to do On maps 1, 2 and 3 keep her on tile 4, or on tile 7 on maps 1 and 2 when the formation allows it. On map 4 prefer tile 4 to tile 2, and on map 5 test tile 7 instead of tile 3.

She investigates nearby enemies together, then the remaining enemies one at a time. Each investigation takes 4.5 seconds. Allied ultimates lower her Detection meter and help her stay hidden, but their timing matters. Landing beside more enemies reduces the time she needs; it does not guarantee she finishes before being revealed.

On map 4, averaged over every recorded enemy formation in the same way, tile 2 lands next to 1.2 enemies and tile 4 next to 2.9. Her landing spot is the matching tile on the enemy half after rotating the board halfway around. Check the actual enemy positions when available; the averages cannot account for a different formation.

Evidence Start whose landing tile touches the most enemies: map 1 tile 7 (2.8); map 2 tile 7 (3.2); map 3 tile 4 (3.1); map 4 tile 4 (2.9); map 5 tile 7 (2.8), averaged over every recorded enemy deployment on the arena

Her results by start tile do not yet show which tile is best low confidence

Tile 4 is 27–22 on map 1, 23–23 on map 2 and 21–9 on map 3. The second choices, tile 5 on maps 1 and 2 (10–1 and 14–8) and tile 6 on map 3 (9–4), have better records from fewer games, and they land next to fewer enemies.

What to do Choose the tile by the enemies it will touch, then check that map’s records in the table above.

Those records mix players, opponents, upgrades and the rest of her team, and the smaller samples are too few to show that the second choices are better tiles. On map 4, tile 2 is 10–5–1t despite landing far from the enemy. The four boards that started her on the forward tile 14 went 3–1, which does not show whether another tile would have worked better. Use nearby-enemy counts to choose a starting placement, then test it against the intended opponent.

Evidence Map 4 forward tile 14: 4 boards, 3–1, landing next to no enemy

The full hero table

Solid chips mean core, outlined chips mean flex. Presence is the share of the 1203 games they appear in; since both sides can field the same hero, it can go as high as 200%. Lift is their win rate minus the average win rate of the players who brought them, a rough way to tell a strong hero from a hero that strong players like.

5 · Caveats #

These results include matches from multiple contributors and leagues, analyzed without replays. They come from only a few of the game's districts. Many matchups have few games. Player skill, hero upgrades and the rules used to group similar teams can affect the results. Ties are excluded from win rates. Read these limits before relying on a particular number.

The caveats in full

The games come from a few districts. Every match was played in the districts the contributors play in, so a record shows how a team did against the opponents in those districts only.

Some players and teams appear far more often than others. A team's results can depend on who used it, their opponents and their upgrades. Games where a player had to reuse the same teams show one team choice several times over, so they are related results. Check the matchup's player and format breakdowns before applying its overall record to another situation.

Tied maps are left out of win rates. The game gives a tied battle to one player, the defending side, and the match lists color a tied map for that player. Winning a map on a tie does not show that the team won the battle, so every win rate leaves ties out.

Missing upgrade levels use match-wide rules. Paragon levels are recorded in 1069 games and refinement levels in 674. If a match has no recorded levels for one upgrade type, every hero is treated as level 4 for that type. If any levels are recorded, a hero without a row is level 0.

The covers the upgrade scale and adjusted ratings; the full ratings show each team's record when it had the upgrade advantage, when it was behind, and when near level.

Teams are grouped by shared heroes. A hero on 80% or more of a group's boards counts as core; 15% to below 80% counts as flex. Every qualifying hero is shown, in order of usage, with no limit on the number of icons. These shares count every recorded appearance, including ties and the matches where players had to reuse the same teams, so a high share means a hero was picked often, whatever the results were. Rarer picks stay in the linked recorded teams, but are omitted from the core and flex lists. Artifacts do not determine the groups.

For common variations, we first find heroes often used together, then count only teams containing every listed hero. A row needs at least eight matching appearances in the team group. +1 flex means one other hero completes the team; expanding a row shows the actual heroes or combinations filling those slots. Rows can overlap, so their counts cannot be added together. Other recorded lineups keeps every exact team outside those rows, including rare picks and losing teams.

The 80% and 15% cutoffs are choices made for this analysis. Broader or narrower groups can change a group's record. Each profile includes the results for its common variations, so you can compare recorded teams without listing every small variation as a separate group.

Flex comparisons can also differ in players, upgrades and opponents. A better record with a hero is worth testing, but does not prove that hero caused the improvement.

Limited evidence means fewer than 30 games with a winner, 10 team selections or 5 players. Concentrated sample means one player contributes at least 35% of appearances, or the two most frequent players contribute at least 60%.

Promising flags a win rate of at least 60% with limited evidence. Narrow use marks a group with a win rate below 50% that the counter test still finds to be a counter to another team, named on its label. Worse than it looks and Better than it looks mark a group whose players had clearly more, or clearly fewer, upgrades than their opponents. Once those upgrade differences are allowed for, its expected win rate against an average team moves by at least 5%, so the raw win rate overstates or understates the team. These labels are hints for reading the table. A team's tier is set separately, and no statistical test is behind a label. A winning record may depend on opponents or upgrades; a losing record can still include a useful counter.

The evidence in each profile shows the record without one most frequent player and at similar upgrades. When SL rules require the same teams for several matches, they count as one team selection per player and map. Separate selections can still share a strategy. Guild membership is not recorded, so these checks cannot identify teams copied within a guild. No team group is excluded for having a losing record.

Each team group gets a rating worked out from its results against the other groups. A team rated r is expected to beat one rated s about r/(r+s) of the time. An average team is rated 1.00. These ratings compare teams with equal upgrades. This gives the expected win rate against an average team in the team groups table.

The rating range in the full ratings comes from redoing the calculation 3,000 times, each time on a random redraw of the 194 groups of related matches. Every match stays together. Matches where a player was required to reuse the same five teams also stay in one group. Each redraw recalculates both the team ratings and the upgrade effect. Tier 1 means at least 80% of those samples put the team above a 55% win rate against an average team at equal upgrades (a rating above 1.22). Tier 3 means at least 80% of them put it below 45% (a rating below 0.82). Every other team is Tier 2: close to average, or with too few games to say. The full ratings show both shares for each team. The tiers only compare the recorded teams with each other. Players still field Tier 3 teams; the label means the team rates below the other recorded teams and says nothing about teams nobody recorded. The same tiers group the teams in the counter ladder. This rating range is a different figure from the win-rate range shown in the team groups table. The same players can still appear in different stages, so results that share a player are still related, and these ranges do not fully allow for that.

The adjusted rating accounts for upgrades. A team can win partly because its heroes have more paragon or EX refinement than the opponent. The adjusted rating includes those differences when estimating team strength.

Both upgrades use one scale, Rivalry points. A paragon level is 4.5 points, the Inspiration/Intimidation it grants (each net point moves healing, shield value, extra Energy gains and buff effects by 1%). A refinement level is 0.9 points, which is its stat gain measured against a paragon level's. The skill effect unlocked at R2 and the Rivalry-mode stats added at R4 are worth 2.1 points each. A fully refined hero is therefore worth 7.7 points more than an unrefined one, about 1.7 paragon levels. The equal-upgrade rating uses each game's combined upgrade gap. The size of that effect is estimated from the 866 decided games where the sides were not equal. Each net point multiplies the advantaged side's odds by ×1.05: ×1.24 for one paragon level on one hero, ×1.44 for one fully refined hero, ×1.53 for a 9-point gap. Odds are wins divided by losses, so a team that wins two games for every one it loses has odds of 2. Multiplying the odds by these amounts is a smaller change than adding the same number of percentage points to a win rate.

Players with more upgrades also tend to have better results. So the rating cannot fully tell how much of their results came from skill and how much from upgrades. A lower adjusted rating suggests that upgrade advantages explain part of the raw record. A higher one suggests the team performed well despite having fewer upgrades.

Tiers use the equal-upgrade ratings from those repeated samples. The unadjusted rating is still shown so the two can be compared. Near level is the team's record in games where the combined upgrade gap was below 4.5 points, equivalent to one paragon level on one hero. The recorded games do not show a winning advantage for gaps that small.

Checking the refinement weight. When the same calculation is run with paragon and refinement weighted separately, it puts a refinement point at 1.11 of a paragon point, based on the 592 decided games where the two sides differed in refinement. That is a single best-guess figure; no range of likely values was worked out for it. Allowing separate effects improves the log-likelihood, a measure of fit to these recorded outcomes, by 0.04. That is little improvement, so these results do not give a strong reason to change the agreed scale. Both calculations still mix the effect of upgrades with differences between players and their teams.

Each diagram shows the group's usual lineup as it was actually placed on a ground in the Supreme League rotation. The team is the five-hero line-up the group fielded most often on those grounds. Each line-up's uses are weighted by how common its heroes are within the group (the Core and Flex percentages multiplied together). This weighting favours the popular flex picks over a placement that one player repeated with an unusual pick. Guild Duel games count when they were played on a ground that is also a Supreme League map (GD-Map1 and GD-Map2 are); Guild Duel's other grounds are left out, because Guild Duel is played far more often and would otherwise decide the board. The ground shown is the one where that team was placed the same way most often, named by its Supreme League map position, and the caption counts uses of that exact placement. The diagram is only an example of where the heroes were placed; it says nothing about which map to choose. A team group never recorded on a Supreme League ground is drawn from all of its boards. Formations recorded on the enemy side are turned around onto the ally half of the board so both sides can be compared.

Placed here is how often a unit used that tile; on N% of boards is how often it appeared. Both refer to the team group on the diagram's map. The core and flex percentages in the main table instead cover all maps.

The phantimal is summoned automatically from the team's factions. You choose its tile, which can affect targeting and artifact effects, but do not select it independently of the heroes.

Testing many matchups can produce chance findings. 38 pairs of team groups had enough games to test in both directions (76 tests). The counter table labels a result as supported when its p-value is below 0.05. The p-value is the chance of a record at least this one-sided turning up if the two teams were really evenly matched. A stricter threshold divides 0.05 by the number of tests to reduce the chance of finding a counter just because many comparisons were made. The counter insights identify which matchups meet that threshold.

Repeated games are not independent examples. The same players can appear many times, sometimes because SL rules require them to reuse the same teams for several matches. Each matchup's details include a recount by whole match, the number of player pairs, and a breakdown when one player accounts for a large share of the games. Those checks help show how much the result depends on repeated games or particular players; they do not remove those effects.

The opponents still matter. A team's record against everyone else includes one-off line-ups, which can make it look stronger. Comparing results on the same maps and allowing for upgrade gaps does not remove differences in player skill or in the exact teams used. The estimated upgrade effect can also include differences between players; these records cannot tell the two apart.

The upgrade effect is estimated. The counter test uses that estimate as if it were exactly right. Its p-values do not allow for that estimate being off, and repeated appearances by the same players and teams also make them less exact. Treat a supported counter as a matchup worth investigating. The p-value does not say how likely you are to win it.

The can also affect the result. Every supported counter was also checked with broader and narrower groups.
